ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Given an equilateral triangle $\triangle ABC$, $M$ is on side $BC$, $MN\perp AC$ at $N$, and intersects $AB$ at point $P$. If $E$, $F$ are respectively on $AB$, $AC$, and $\triangle MEF$ is an equilateral triangle, when the value of $\frac{S_{\triangle MEF}}{S_{\triangle ABC}}$ is minimal, what is the value of $\frac{BM}{BC}$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: \textbf{Solution:} When the value of $\frac{S_{\triangle MEF}}{S_{\triangle ABC}}$ is minimal, $\frac{BM}{BC}=\boxed{\frac{1}{2}}$.

method.method_draft: Synthetic trigonometric route. Let BC=a, BM=x, CM=a-x, and let the side length of equilateral triangle MEF be l. Define alpha=angle BME and beta=angle FMC. From the straight line B-M-C and angle EMF=60 degrees, the upper-half-plane angles satisfy alpha+60+beta=180, so alpha+beta=120. In triangle BME, angle EBM=60 degrees because BA and BC form the equilateral angle, and ME=l. By the sine rule, x=BM=l sin(120-alpha)/sin60. Similarly, in triangle CMF, angle MCF=60 degrees and beta=120-alpha, so a-x=CM=l sin(alpha)/sin60. Add the two equations: a=l[sin(120-alpha)+sin alpha]/sin60. Thus l/a=sin60/[sin(120-alpha)+sin alpha]. The area ratio equals (l/a)^2, so minimizing area is equivalent to minimizing l/a, i.e. maximizing sin(120-alpha)+sin alpha=2 sin60 cos(60-alpha). This is maximized when alpha=60 degrees. Then x=BM=l and the sum gives a=2l, so BM/BC=x/a=1/2.
